raw_response:
I've been working this land for 40 years. My father farmed before me. I don't need to think too hard about what to plant — I know this soil, I know what the weather does here in Quzhou, and I know what prices have looked like at the market. My children have told me some of them want to work in town. That means I do more myself, and I keep things manageable.

My 60 mu is split up the way it has been for years. Twenty-five mu I do wheat in winter, then turn around and plant maize on the same ground after the June harvest — that land works hard but it's flat and the well can reach it. Twenty mu goes to cotton, which is a headache with the insects but the buyers still come and the price is decent. Fifteen mu I put in spring peanut — the soil in that corner is sandy, peanut does well there, and I can save seed from last year.

For wheat, I'll plough in October, use the improved variety the seed station sells — Jimai or Shijiazhuang 8, whatever is available. I apply base fertilizer before planting, then top dress at jointing. I run the pump three times: before winter sets in, at jointing, and at heading. I spray twice — once for aphids in spring, once for rust if I see it.

After wheat harvest, I go straight into maize. I don't plough — just rotary till and drill hybrid seed. Maize is easier. Two irrigations, two pesticide passes for corn borer and aphids.

Cotton goes in April. I use hybrid Bt seed, it's more expensive but I spray less for bollworm. Still, aphids are bad some years, so I plan for four or five pesticide applications. Cotton needs water — I irrigate four times. I plough in early spring.

Peanut I plant late April. I saved seed from last year's harvest. Peanut doesn't need much nitrogen since it fixes its own. I focus on phosphorus and potassium. Two or three irrigations depending on rain, and I usually only spray once or twice.
